networking-fundamentals-sr4-12.reason: explanation_error: old explanation implied IIDs never expose hardware addresses; RFC 7136 only says IID bits have no generic semantics and must be treated as opaque by third parties. (final: keep)
networking-fundamentals-sr4-12.statement: RFC 7136 treats an IPv6 interface identifier as a coded description of the interface's hardware address.
networking-fundamentals-sr4-12.explanation: RFC 7136 says the bits of an interface identifier have no generic meaning, and third parties must treat the whole value as an opaque bit string.
networking-fundamentals-sr4-12.misconception: Interface identifier bits encode hardware properties.

source.title: RFC 7136: Significance of IPv6 Interface Identifiers

networking-fundamentals-sr5-11.reason: source_problem: cited Section 6.1 never says stateless DHCPv6 gives no addresses; Section 1 does. Explanation aligned to Section 1. (final: keep)
networking-fundamentals-sr5-11.statement: A host uses stateless DHCPv6 to request an IPv6 address after processing a Router Advertisement.
networking-fundamentals-sr5-11.explanation: Stateless DHCPv6 provides only other configuration options, with no addresses or prefixes, so the server keeps no state. The host gets its IPv6 addresses by another mechanism.
networking-fundamentals-sr5-11.misconception: Stateless DHCPv6 provides IPv6 address leases.

source.title: RFC 9915: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol for IPv6 (DHCPv6)

networking-fundamentals-sr7-05.reason: ambiguous: 'registered' clashes with the RFC 6335 term (179 is a System Port, not a Registered/User Port). (final: fixed)
networking-fundamentals-sr7-05.statement: A BGP speaker listens on TCP port 179 for the connections its peers open to start BGP sessions.
networking-fundamentals-sr7-05.explanation: BGP runs over TCP. RFC 4271 has every BGP implementation listen on TCP port 179 for incoming connections in addition to trying to connect to its peers.

networking-fundamentals-sr7-11.reason: ambiguous: 'by default' read as real implementation behaviour, where many speakers still accept EBGP routes; now scoped to RFC 8212 and the 'by default'/'before' tells removed. (final: fixed)
networking-fundamentals-sr7-11.statement: Under RFC 8212, a BGP speaker lacking an explicit import policy for an EBGP peer considers that peer's routes eligible.
networking-fundamentals-sr7-11.explanation: RFC 8212 makes routes from an EBGP peer ineligible in the Decision Process until an explicit import policy is applied, though a speaker may offer an option to deviate.
networking-fundamentals-sr7-11.misconception: EBGP routes are used until an import filter is added.

networking-fundamentals-sr11-08.reason: ambiguous: 'can cache ... by default' could be defended as True because RFC 8767 says only lowercase 'should not be cached'. (final: fixed)
networking-fundamentals-sr11-08.statement: A DNS resolver keeps a record that arrived with a TTL of zero in its cache to answer the next query for that name.
networking-fundamentals-sr11-08.explanation: RFC 8767's TTL definition says a zero TTL limits a record to the transaction in progress and that the record should not be cached, not even for stale fallback.
networking-fundamentals-sr11-08.misconception: A zero TTL means the record never expires, as in some other caches.

source.title: RFC 8767: Serving Stale Data to Improve DNS Resiliency

networking-fundamentals-sr12-05.reason: ambiguous: narrated an action that real MTAs often tolerate instead of the RFC 2181 rule; 'directly' tell removed. (final: fixed)
networking-fundamentals-sr12-05.statement: RFC 2181 lets the host named in a domain's MX record be a CNAME alias that points to the mail server.
networking-fundamentals-sr12-05.explanation: RFC 2181 says an MX target must not be an alias but must have its own address records, because additional-section processing does not follow CNAMEs.
networking-fundamentals-sr12-05.misconception: An MX target may be a CNAME alias.

source.title: RFC 2181: Clarifications to the DNS Specification

networking-fundamentals-sr12-07.reason: weak_card (definition card, wrong actor), rewritten instead of dropped: dropping 06, 07 and 11 would leave r12 at 3T/6F; verifier's replacement confirmed in RFC 1034 Section 4.3.5 and shortened to keep T/F lengths level. (final: keep)
networking-fundamentals-sr12-07.statement: A secondary DNS server compares its SOA serial with the primary's to detect a changed zone.
networking-fundamentals-sr12-07.explanation: RFC 1034 has secondaries poll the primary for the zone's SOA record; an advanced serial means the zone changed, so the secondary fetches a new copy.

networking-fundamentals-sr13-06.reason: source_problem: Section 1.2 does not mention AEAD; Section 5.2 states it. Explanation extended with the reason. (final: keep)
networking-fundamentals-sr13-06.statement: A TLS 1.3 endpoint negotiates a separate MAC algorithm for record protection.
networking-fundamentals-sr13-06.explanation: TLS 1.3 models every record cipher as AEAD, one operation that both encrypts and authenticates, so records need no separately negotiated MAC.
networking-fundamentals-sr13-06.misconception: Record protection negotiates a separate MAC.

networking-fundamentals-sr13-08.reason: ambiguous: without supported_versions a TLS 1.3-capable server negotiates TLS 1.2 or earlier the RFC 5246 way; statement now scoped to a ClientHello that carries supported_versions. (final: fixed)
networking-fundamentals-sr13-08.statement: To negotiate TLS 1.3, a server reads the version the client offers from the legacy_version field of the ClientHello.
networking-fundamentals-sr13-08.explanation: A server negotiates TLS 1.3 only through supported_versions, and when a ClientHello carries that extension, the server must not use legacy_version for version negotiation.
networking-fundamentals-sr13-08.misconception: legacy_version still drives version negotiation when supported_versions is present.

networking-fundamentals-sr14-12.reason: tell: removes 'automatically' from a false card and puts 'must' in a false card (must/should/at least were 8 of 8 true). Fact and answer unchanged. (final: keep)
networking-fundamentals-sr14-12.statement: A QUIC sender must resend DATAGRAM frames when their packets are declared lost.
networking-fundamentals-sr14-12.explanation: QUIC's DATAGRAM extension leaves lost datagrams unretransmitted, even though their packets elicit acknowledgments.
networking-fundamentals-sr14-12.misconception: The QUIC transport retransmits lost DATAGRAM frames.

source.title: RFC 9221: An Unreliable Datagram Extension to QUIC

networking-fundamentals-sr6-03.reason: tell: puts 'must' in a false card and replaces the opaque 'undeliverable ICMP error'; fact (no ICMP error about an ICMP error) and answer unchanged. URL anchor fixed: the RFC 1122 HTML has only top-level section ids. (final: fixed)
networking-fundamentals-sr6-03.statement: In IPv4, a host must report a problem with a received ICMP error message by sending an ICMP error.
networking-fundamentals-sr6-03.explanation: RFC 1122 says a host must not send an ICMP error message as the result of receiving an ICMP error message, so a faulty ICMP error is never answered with another one.
networking-fundamentals-sr6-03.misconception: ICMP error messages receive further ICMP errors when they cause a problem.

networking-fundamentals-sr8-08.reason: tell: removes 'automatically' (0 true / 2 false); fact and answer unchanged; anchor points at the RFC 6335 Section 7.2 sentence. (final: fixed)
networking-fundamentals-sr8-08.statement: When IANA assigns a port to a service that asked only for UDP, it also assigns that number for TCP.
networking-fundamentals-sr8-08.explanation: Since RFC 6335, IANA assigns a port only for the transport protocols requested and marks the number Reserved for the others; older assignments often cover both.
networking-fundamentals-sr8-08.misconception: A UDP port assignment automatically includes TCP.

source.title: RFC 6335: Service Name and Transport Protocol Port Number Registry Management

networking-fundamentals-sr5-02.reason: tell: removes 'directly' (0 true / 2 false); fact (rebinding broadcasts) and answer unchanged. (final: keep)
networking-fundamentals-sr5-02.statement: A DHCPv4 client in the rebinding state unicasts its DHCPREQUEST to the server that granted the lease.
networking-fundamentals-sr5-02.explanation: At T2, the client broadcasts DHCPREQUEST so any available server can extend the lease. Contacting the original server belongs to the earlier renewal stage.
networking-fundamentals-sr5-02.misconception: Rebinding contacts the original lease server just like renewal.

networking-fundamentals-sr2-02.reason: tell: removes 'ordinary' (0 true / 5 false) and 'its own', and adds a hedge verb to a false card; fact and answer unchanged. (final: fixed)
networking-fundamentals-sr2-02.statement: In an IPv4 /24 subnet, a host can take the all-zero host part as its unicast address.
networking-fundamentals-sr2-02.explanation: RFC 1122 does not permit an all-zero host part in an IPv4 address outside its listed special cases, so the .0 address of a /24 is not a host unicast address.
networking-fundamentals-sr2-02.misconception: The subnet address serves as an ordinary unicast host address.
